There's a great many games I could use here, but how about a "rival" game. Dragon Age: Inquisition, thus far, has for free additional content:

  • The Red Lyrium Reaper weapons (all you need to do for that is play the online minigame)
  • Item storage in Skyhold
  • Armor tinting for all party members
  • The Black Emporium (with new weapons and the Mirror of Transformation)
  • Two thrones (Fereldan and Kirkwall) available to players of the previous games
  • The Destruction MP DLC (new areas, enemies, gear)
  • The Dragonslayer MP DLC (new map, three new unique characters, high dragon battles)

That's all divided across six patches/DLCs.

Compare to The Witcher 3's DLCs:

  • A half-dozen DLCs that consist of one outfit (either a purely-cosmetic outfit for an NPC or mediocre gear)
  • A handful of weapons (about half of the Reapers/Black Emporium gear combined)
  • A reskinned deck of cards
  • A bunch of quests with inconsequential outcomes and pitiful loot
  • Horse armor. Literally.

And all of that apparently takes sixteen DLCs.

There's a difference between the two developers:

  • BioWare introduced most of this stuff without making a big deal of it, with a fair amount of the content introduced in patches that also dealt with glitches and balancing
  • CD Projekt made a big deal out of their DLC, focusing on the inflated number (which is solely due to putting very little content into each individual DLC) and spending more time on the "one outfit" DLC than fixing glitches that can render the main quest unfinishable

In short: Free DLC isn't something new. Blatantly trying to pander to the rabid anti-DLC crowd with tiny scraps, while pretending that what they are doing is something special, is.

This works with beef, chicken, pork, goat, and lamb.

How it works:Baking soda will increase the alkalinity of the protein strands. When meat is cooked, the protein coils and tightens. Baking soda helps prevent this.

The decreased acidity will help the meat retain more moisture which makes more tender meat.

This method works better with sliced meats, since it really only works on the surface. 1/4 in slices are the best.

You can do it with roasts and thicker sliced steaks, but it is less effective.

Technique:Take 1 teaspoon for every pound of meat, mix baking soda with enough water to cover the meat.

Your aiming for a 5% solution, which gives a PH of 8.

Let meat stand for 15 minutes, rinse meat thoroughly.

Disadvantages: This will create a grey color on the meat. This can be overcome with a good sear.

This creates an alkaline taste to the meat. This can be overcome with mixing 1 lemon's worth of juice (3 tablespoons) with enough water to cover the meat. Coat the meat with the acidulated water. Let stand for 2 minutes. Rinse again.

The acid corrects the alkalinity by coverting the NaHCO3 (sodium bicarbonate) into H2CO3 (carbonic acid). This breaks into CO2 (carbon dioxide) and H20 (water).
